demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about why the event has happened to me
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger

issues.item: Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategy items imply an ongoing external danger/escape-monitoring profile more typical of fear-based threat from assault, accident re-exposure, or unsafe environments. That does not fit well with the trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another,' where the central disturbance is more plausibly guilt, responsibility, and intrusive memory rather than escape positioning.

Mirror checking is not clinically coherent with the rest of this profile. For a trauma involving accidentally causing serious injury to another, the other selected items center on dissociative/fragmented memory and guilt-focused rumination/meaning seeking. Mirror checking instead suggests appearance/body/reality checking behavior that is not supported by the memory items, not linked by the formulation's active edges, and is hard to explain as part of the same PTSD presentation here.

vignette: Ms. Te Mana, a 61-year-old security guard from Oceania, has been grappling with profound distress following an incident where she accidentally caused serious injury to another person during her shift at work. The event still haunts her, but much of it remains shrouded in gaps and fragments, which only exacerbate the anguish. On that fateful evening, Ms. Te Mana was patrolling a dimly lit warehouse when she heard an unusual noise. As she approached the source of the commotion, she stepped on a loose board, causing her to slip and fall onto another guard, breaking his leg in the process. The memory of this incident is fraught with gaps; there are moments that feel like they belong to someone else rather than herself. At times, when she tries to recall what happened, it feels as if she were observing a stranger in a film, leaving her feeling detached and numb. The gaps and alienation Ms. Te Mana experiences with the memory drive her into a relentless cycle of meaning-seeking and self-blame. She thinks about why this event has happened to her and what she could have done differently to prevent it. This constant rumination leads her to overanalyze every detail, hoping that by reconstructing the sequence of events, she might find some answers or a way to make sense of the trauma. However, as she delves deeper into these maladaptive strategies, the memory becomes even more fractured and disconnected from her own identity. The self-blame only deepens her conviction that the event is her fault, leading her to constantly scrutinize every action and decision she made before and during the incident. This obsessive overthinking further distorts her recollection of the event, making it feel increasingly distant and unreal. Ms. Te Mana’s work as a security guard has become unbearably stressful. The warehouse where the accident occurred is now filled with triggers that remind her of the event—every creaking floorboard and shadow casts doubt on whether she can ever be trusted again. Her colleagues have noticed her distress, but they do not fully understand the depth of her anguish. Over time, Ms. Te Mana’s preoccupation with understanding the accident has seeped into every aspect of her life. She often finds herself lost in thought during her shifts, trying to piece together what she can remember and what she cannot. This distraction has led to some near-misses at work, further fueling her anxiety that another incident might occur due to her inattention. What frightens Ms. Te Mana most is the fear of losing control again and causing harm to others or herself. She recognizes that her constant rumination and self-blame are not helping but feels trapped by them. The more she tries to make sense of what happened, the less coherent her memory becomes, reinforcing her belief that she should have known better. Finally, after months of struggling with these thoughts and feelings, Ms. Te Mana has decided to seek help. She hopes to find a way to understand and process the event without feeling overwhelmed by guilt and self-doubt. Her primary fear is continuing to live in this constant cycle of doubt and pain, but she also holds hope that therapy can provide her with tools to regain control over her thoughts and memories. Ms. Te Mana’s journey toward healing begins with a desire to break free from the relentless cycle of rumination and memory gaps, finding a way to integrate the past without it dominating her present life.
